newsitem.title: UK: Work on U.K. end of Interconnector gas line begins.
newsitem.headline: Work on U.K. end of Interconnector gas line begins.

text.p: Work on the Interconnector, the new pipeline taking British natural gas to continental Europe, began at the U.K. terminal of Bacton in Norfolk this week.

The pipeline should go into operation on October 1, 1998, said Paul Convert, project manager of Interconnector (UK) Ltd, which is building the line. Work on the Belgian outlet terminal in Zeebrugge began in mid-October.
Convert and other Interconnector officials were speaking to journalists at a briefing on the project.
The 235-km, 40-inch pipeline with a capacity of 20 billion cubic metres (bcm) a year will give Britain a market for its gas surplus.

But in the case of rising domestic demand and declining production, the Interconnector will give Britain access to 8.5 bcm a year of gas from other sources. The biggest suppliers of gas to Europe are Russia, Algeria and Norway.
Technically, the Interconnector poses few problems, said Jan Raven, Offshore Manager of Interconnector (UK) Ltd.
Raven said the line will be laid by two barges, of which one semi-submersible will do nearly all the work.
Another flat-bottomed barge -- described by Raven as "very old fashioned" -- will be used to lay the pipeline close to shore as this avoids the need to dredge expensive access channels.
Pipelaying will take about two and a half months next summer, at a rate of around 100 km a month. A total of 130,000 tonnes of pipe in nearly 20,000 sections will be laid.

The route of the link will not follow a straight line, as there is a military training area to be avoided and the line is sticking to only British and Belgian territorial waters, steering clear of a disputed offshore border between Belgium and the Netherlands.

Raven said that because of so-called "sand waves" on the sea bed, the line cannot be unsupported for long stretches and the line will have to be laid in a trench across these to prevent the line undergoing stress.

Roger Cornish, managing director of Interconnector (UK) Ltd, said little technical innovation is required to build the line, and said that "the alliances (of partners involved in construction) are the most innovative aspects of the project."
Onshore, the project uses existing technology, onshore manager Tony McEwan said. At Bacton, gas will be compressed to a pressure of 140 bar and cooled before entering the Interconnector.
Because the Belgian grid operates under variable pressure of 55 to 80 bar, the gas will be heated and subjected to flow control before entering the grid.
McEwan said he was leaving a large area undeveloped at Zeebrugge to build compression facilities in future to allow gas to be sent from Zeebrugge to Bacton.
All construction work will be completed by June 1998, allowing three months for testing before the start up.

Participants in the Interconnector, which will cost 450 million stg to build, are Amerada Hess (five percent), BP (10 percent), British Gas (40 percent), Du Pont's Conoco (10 percent), Distrigaz (five percent), Elf (10 percent), Gazprom (10 percent), National Power (five percent), and Ruhrgas (five percent).
